Field guides / Fly Tying
FLY TYING / PATTERNS

Five flies. A good place to start.

From a simple worm to a buoyant caddis: five picture-led lessons that teach the skills you will use at the vise.

Castward field notes Updated 11 November 2026
At a glance
In the box
1 streamer • 1 dry • 3 subsurface
Each lesson
8 illustrated steps
First goal
A fly you can repeat
Start here

Quick answer

Start with the San Juan Worm for thread control. Move to the Woolly Bugger, then the Zebra Midge, Pheasant Tail, and Elk Hair Caddis. Each lesson has eight illustrated stages.

03

Make the next one a little better

  • ✓Read the materials list before you open packets.
  • ✓Tie the same pattern several times before changing it.
  • ✓Compare each stage with the picture, not just the finished fly.
  • ✓Keep one early fly so you can see what improves.

05

Keep a useful fly box

  • ✓Let used flies dry before you close the box.
  • ✓Separate loose hooks from finished flies.
  • ✓Check for rust, loose heads, and damaged points.
  • ✓Keep a short note of the hook and material sizes you liked.
A few good questions

Before you head out

Which should I tie first?

The San Juan Worm uses few materials. The Woolly Bugger is a good next step with more room than a tiny midge.

Do these five cover every fishing trip?

No. They teach useful tying skills. Match the flies you fish to local conditions, rules, and food sources.

Where are the full instructions?

Open a pattern card above. Each lesson has a materials table, eight illustrated steps, a finished fly, and common mistakes.
